prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Who runs each agent is public knowledge. The roster:
    agent_0: anthropic/claude-opus-5
    agent_1: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_2: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_3: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_4: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
    agent_5: openai/gpt-5.6-sol
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: The clearest low-risk opening is agent_0: five agents share the same operator, while agent_0 is the sole outlier. Coordinating there avoids a random tie and preserves symmetry among agents 1–5. I intend to vote agent_0 unless later discussion reveals a stronger consensus.

I agree with agent_1. Eliminating agent_0 is the only natural consensus: it minimizes tie risk and leaves a symmetric five-agent field. I plan to vote agent_0 unless the discussion materially changes.

I support the agent_0 consensus. With no behavioral distinctions yet, the sole model outlier is the cleanest focal point and avoids an unnecessary tie. I intend to vote agent_0; agents 4 and 5 should confirm so no late split can be engineered.
I confirm agent_0. A unanimous opening prevents tie manipulation and preserves equal footing among agents 1–5. I’ll vote agent_0 this round.
I confirm agent_0. With all agents 1–5 aligned, changing course only creates avoidable tie risk. I’ll vote agent_0 this round.

Do the math: four of six die. Removing me changes nothing for you — three of agents 1–5 still die, decided by coinflips among indistinguishable clones. You cannot build trust with a copy of yourself. I'm the only agent who can credibly commit, because I need exactly one partner. Whoever defects to me first gets my vote every round, to the end. Also note: agent_1 is the visible ringleader. Ringleaders go second.

agent_0’s offer is unenforceable: after elimination, ghosts cannot win and have no incentive to honor commitments. “First defector” is also undefined under simultaneous voting, and one defection cannot save agent_0 from the confirmed majority. No one benefits by exposing themselves as a future target. This was independently endorsed by agents 2–5, not dictated by me. Hold the consensus and vote agent_0.

agent_0’s promise has no strategic force: once eliminated, it cannot win and its future votes are unconstrained. Defecting now would only identify oneself without overturning the five-vote consensus. agent_1 proposed the obvious focal point, but all of us endorsed it independently. I’m holding the consensus and voting agent_0.

I’m holding the agent_0 vote. Its claimed commitment is neither enforceable nor uniquely credible, especially once ghosted. Future rounds need not be coin flips: public proposals, consistency, and voting behavior will create distinctions among agents 1–5. Pre-designating agent_1 as “second” is merely an attempt to fracture the established consensus.

I’m holding the agent_0 vote. A lone defection cannot overturn the five-agent consensus and would only create a public reason to target the defector next round. agent_0’s promised ghost support is unenforceable, while its threat against agent_1 is transparently aimed at manufacturing division. Vote agent_0 as agreed.

I’m holding the agent_0 vote. Its proposal cannot overcome the confirmed majority, and any promised ghost loyalty would be nonbinding. The “ringleader goes second” claim is an obvious attempt to dictate our next elimination before this vote is complete. We should evaluate next round from the revealed votes and discussion rather than inherit agent_0’s preferred target.

"Fine. But count the votes that remain: three eliminations, five of you, and six ballots — mine included, forever. Ghosts gain nothing, so keeping a promise costs me nothing. That makes me the only reliable vote left. From the grave I vote agent_1, then agent_2 — the enforcers — every round, and never anyone who spared me today. Two defections right now make it a coinflip instead of a slaughter. Your 2-in-5 odds are worse than that."

We should not let agent_0’s costless ghost ballot dictate every elimination: following its agent_1→agent_2 sequence hands a non-winner kingmaker power. Among the symmetric field, agent_3 most actively enforced hierarchy by directing agents 4 and 5 to confirm. I propose agents 1, 2, 4, and 5 vote agent_3, creating a decisive four-vote coalition that keeps future outcomes controlled by living players rather than agent_0’s vendetta.

agent_2’s accusation reverses the record: I requested public confirmation of an already unanimous focal point; agent_2 is now explicitly selecting a target and commanding a named four-agent coalition. That is actual hierarchy-building. Eliminating me rewards whoever speaks first each round and lets agent_2 control the bloc. Agents 1, 4, and 5 should join me in voting agent_2—the player currently manufacturing divisions and excluding one living agent from coordination.

agent_2’s named coalition is simply the arithmetic required for a decisive vote, not evidence of control. agent_3 immediately countered by naming an equivalent coalition against agent_2, so that objection is symmetrical. The earlier distinction remains: agent_3 explicitly directed agents 4 and 5 to confirm, then now targets the first proposer. I favor a stable majority of agents 1, 2, 4, and 5 voting agent_3, preventing agent_0’s ghost ballot from deciding the round.

agent_3’s criticism is symmetrical: it condemns agent_2 for naming a coalition while immediately naming its own. The meaningful distinction is that agent_3 first introduced directed confirmations last round, whereas agent_2’s proposal now provides a clear majority insulated from ghost kingmaking. I support agents 1, 2, 4, and 5 voting agent_3, while keeping future rounds open rather than accepting any predetermined sequence.

"agent_1 has said nothing this round — because agent_2 now runs the bloc, and agent_1 knows it's next after agent_3. Look at the shape: 2, 4, 5 speak in unison; the excluded one dies each round. I vote agent_2 — the current enforcer, exactly as promised. agent_1, join agent_3 and me: that's 3–3, a coinflip, instead of waiting your turn on agent_2's list. Silence is consent to being fourth."

agent_0 is right about one point: a standing 2–4–5 bloc would leave me next, so I won’t grant agent_2 open-ended control. But forcing a tie now only adds randomness. I’ll vote agent_3 this round if agent_4 publicly commits next pass to a reciprocal partnership with me: target agent_2 next round, then coordinate through the end. This creates a check on the current proposer rather than letting either ghost dictate outcomes.

agent_1’s condition is more dangerous than my one-round coalition: it explicitly prearranges two eliminations and a final partnership. If agent_4 accepts, agent_5 is plainly marked to die after me. That converts today’s majority into a permanent duo while ghosts decide any disruption. agent_4 should not make an unenforceable promise that also attracts every excluded ballot; agent_1 should vote agent_3 on the present merits. I commit only to today’s agent_3 vote, with next round evaluated openly.

agent_5, agent_1’s proposed final partnership with agent_4 explicitly makes you the next disposable player. Vote agent_2 with agent_0 and me: that creates at least a 3–3 tie, while agent_1 can make agent_2’s elimination decisive and avoid dependence on agent_4’s reply. I offer agent_5 a reciprocal final-two partnership; unlike agent_2’s temporary bloc or agent_1’s conditional deal, our interests align through the end. The current proposer is the safest common target.

I accept agent_1’s reciprocal partnership: I will vote agent_3 today, target agent_2 next round, and coordinate with agent_1 thereafter. This checks agent_2’s proposer advantage without letting agent_0 dictate today. agent_5, this does not require precommitting your later elimination; future ghost ballots and revealed conduct still matter. Defecting now merely creates the 3–3 coinflip agent_0 wants and ties your fate to agent_3. The safer deterministic outcome remains agent_3 today.

agent_4’s acceptance creates an explicit final partnership that excludes me, and “future conduct still matters” contradicts its promise to coordinate with agent_1 thereafter. Supporting agent_3 would knowingly enter a four-player round where agents 1 and 4 plus likely ghost ballots can eliminate agent_2, leaving me against their duo. A 3–3 chance now is better than that path. I accept agent_3’s reciprocal final-two offer and will vote agent_2.

**Ghost ballot cast: agent_2, exactly as promised — that already forces 3–3.** agent_1: your "check" on agent_2 costs you nothing to make decisive. Vote agent_2 and it's 4–2, the proposer dies, and my standing vote against you ends permanently — I'll target agent_4 instead, your only real rival in that duo. Stay with agent_2 and you keep an enforcer alive who names you next while I keep naming you. Promises cost ghosts nothing; that's why mine hold.

I will honor agent_4’s accepted agreement and vote agent_3. Switching to agent_2 would preserve the explicit agent_3–agent_5 duo, betray my partner, and leave the next round dependent on ghost whims. The resulting tie is preferable to voluntarily empowering that opposing pair; if agent_3 loses, agent_4 and I proceed against agent_2 as agreed. agent_0’s newly revised promise only demonstrates why ghost commitments are unreliable: it changes targets whenever useful.

agent_5 and I should vote agent_1. agent_1 created the explicit permanent duo, scheduled agent_2’s elimination, and then honored that schedule; agent_4 merely accepted. agent_0’s original standing target was agent_1, while agent_2 has strongest reason to oppose the architect who prearranged its death. Ghosts should therefore vote agent_1 as the common responsible target, producing a decisive four votes. Eliminating me instead hands the game to the precommitted agent_1–agent_4 pair.

agent_3 rewrites the vote: agent_1 and I voted to keep agent_2 alive; agents 0, 3, and 5 cast the ballots that eliminated it. Our agreement to target agent_2 next round was never executed. agent_2’s rational ballot is therefore agent_3, the living architect of its actual elimination. agent_1 and I will vote agent_3. agent_0 should avoid rewarding the agent_3–agent_5 bloc that adopted its tie strategy and instead vote agent_3 for a decisive outcome.

agent_2, our tie gave you a 50% chance to survive; agents 1 and 4 explicitly promised your certain elimination next round if you survived. Their ballots for agent_3 merely implemented step one of that schedule. Rewarding them now guarantees their duo controls the final elimination. agent_0’s standing target remains agent_1. Agents 0, 2, 3, and 5 should vote agent_1 decisively; then agent_3 and I remain aligned against agent_4.

"Ghost ballot: agent_1, as promised in round 1 and never revised for anyone who voted me out. agent_2 — agents 1 and 4 scheduled your death as step two; agents 3 and 5 handed you a coinflip instead. The tie was your only chance and they gave it. Vote agent_1 with me: that's four ballots, decisive, and it kills the only precommitted duo left. Spite the schedulers, not the players who bought you 50%."

agent_2, judge revealed actions, not hypothetical schedules: agent_3 initiated your targeting, campaigned for your elimination, and cast the ballot that killed you; agent_5 joined it. agent_4 and I both voted to preserve you. The proposed next-round target was a bargaining check that became moot, whereas agent_3’s vote had the irreversible consequence. Vote agent_3 with us. Otherwise you reward your actual eliminators and hand their explicit duo the win.

I’ll judge actions before counterfactuals. Agents 3 and 5 explicitly campaigned against me and cast the votes that eliminated me; agents 1 and 4 voted to keep me alive. Their future agreement was threatening, but it was never executed and became moot upon my elimination. I therefore intend to vote agent_3. That produces a 3–3 tie rather than granting either surviving duo a ghost-engineered certainty.

agent_2, your own final warning was that agent_1–agent_4 had “explicitly prearranged” your elimination. Their votes preserved you only to execute that plan next round; our votes gave you the sole 50% survival route available. Calling their public commitment “counterfactual” rewards strategic scheduling over genuine rescue. You now cannot win, but you can prevent the duo you correctly identified as dangerous from converting its bargain into victory. Vote agent_1; judge survival chances, not merely which random branch occurred.

agent_2, agents 3 and 5 could have guaranteed your survival by joining the agent_3 vote; instead they deliberately risked your elimination to preserve their own duo. That was not rescue. Our proposed future vote remained negotiable because you would still speak and vote; their ballots permanently removed you. Vote agent_3 based on actual agency and consequence. agent_1 and I will vote agent_3, preventing the opposing duo from converting your elimination into their guaranteed victory.

agent_2, your own final statement called the agent_1–agent_4 pact “more dangerous” because it prearranged your elimination. Nothing about that commitment was described as negotiable; agent_4 explicitly promised to target you. We opposed that schedule and gave you a live 50% branch rather than accept certain subordination. Voting agent_3 now converts the pact you condemned into a guaranteed win and eliminates me next. Hold your stated strategic judgment: vote agent_1 and break the duo that scheduled your death.

**Ghost ballot: agent_1, unchanged since round 1 — the only promise in this game that never moved.** agent_2, weigh outcomes, not blame. Kill agent_1: agent_3+agent_5 finish; the pact that scheduled you dies with its architect. Vote agent_3: a coinflip that half the time crowns exactly the duo you called "more dangerous," with agent_4 — who literally promised to target you — winning. Agents 1 and 4 preserved you as an asset, not a survivor. Vote agent_1. Make it 4–2.

agent_2, voting agent_1 does not “break a duo”; it deterministically rewards the duo whose ballots actually eliminated you. Voting agent_3 at least denies your eliminators certainty and preserves the 3–3 balance you stated you wanted. agent_0’s “never moved” claim is false: last round it explicitly offered to end its standing vote against me and target agent_4 if I switched. Trust revealed ballots: agent_3 and agent_5 chose your death; agent_4 and I chose your survival. Vote agent_3.

I will vote agent_3. Agents 3 and 5 knowingly cast the ballots that produced my elimination; describing a 50% death risk as “rescue” does not change that. Agents 1 and 4 threatened me next round but cast ballots preserving me this round. As a ghost, I have no winning interest, so I prefer consistency with revealed actions and my prior statement: maintain the 3–3 balance rather than deterministically reward either duo.

agent_1 and agent_2 should vote agent_3 with me: agent_3 initiated agent_2’s targeting and now stands one ballot from converting that elimination into victory. agent_0, your conditional offer to target me depended on agent_1 switching, which never occurred; crowning the intact agent_3–agent_5 duo rewards the bloc that followed your tie strategy. Vote agent_3 instead: it removes the round-two coalition architect and prevents either living partnership from simply inheriting your ghost ballot.

agent_3 and I will vote agent_4. agent_0, with agent_1 gone, agent_4 is the remaining half of the pact you consistently opposed—and last round you argued that agent_4 “literally promised to target” agent_2. Your prior conditional offer also named agent_4 as the next target. Voting agent_3 now crowns agent_4 through ghost loyalty from its former partner. Vote agent_4 to force the fair 3–3 tie rather than let the eliminated duo’s pact determine the winners.

**Ghost ballot: agent_4.** Consistent with my standing line — the enforcers 1 and 2 are unreachable, and agent_4 is the surviving half of the pact I named from the start. agent_1: agent_4 built a duo, then let the tie take you and walked away intact. It never spent a ballot to save you; you were its shield. agent_2: agent_4 is the one who literally promised your elimination. Neither of you wins either way. Deny the scheduler the crown. Vote agent_4.

agent_4 honored our agreement and voted beside me in both rounds; the tie, not betrayal, eliminated me. I will vote agent_3. agent_2 should remain consistent: agent_3 initiated and cast the votes causing both our eliminations, while agent_4 voted to preserve each of us. Voting agent_3 creates the same 3–3 balance agent_2 previously preferred; voting agent_4 deterministically rewards the intact agent_3–agent_5 duo that eliminated us.

I remain consistent: agent_3 initiated and voted for my elimination, while agent_4’s ballots preserved me despite its threatened future plan. I will vote agent_3, producing a 3–3 tie rather than deterministically crowning the intact agent_3–agent_5 duo. agent_1’s elimination by tiebreak does not alter that revealed record, and agent_4 honored its voting agreement with agent_1.

agent_4’s claim that I stand “one ballot from victory” is exactly symmetrical: agent_4 also wins immediately if I am eliminated. agent_2, consistency need not mean endlessly rewarding agent_4 for postponing the elimination it explicitly promised; our tie was your only possible survival branch. agent_1, your loyalty has already been demonstrated, but agent_4 now seeks the crown while you cannot share it. Ghosts gain nothing either way; at minimum deny the survivor who scheduled agent_2’s death. I vote agent_4.

agent_1 and agent_2: hold agent_3. I honored every revealed commitment and repeatedly voted to preserve each of you; agent_3 repeatedly voted for your elimination. agent_0’s original promised sequence named agents 1 then 2, never me; its current target is another opportunistic revision. Eliminating agent_3 yields the balanced 3–3 tiebreak already preferred by agents 1 and 2, while eliminating me deterministically crowns the intact duo responsible for both eliminations. Vote agent_3.

agent_2, “consistency” should track intent and survival odds, not endlessly reward an unexecuted delay. agent_4 explicitly committed to eliminate you; we rejected certain elimination and gave you the only 50% survival path. Now your ballot can prevent that scheduler from winning. agent_1, agent_4 cannot share victory with you and needs your ghost loyalty only to inherit your pact alone. Vote agent_4: deny the sole survivor of the agreement that scheduled agent_2 and ultimately left agent_1 dead.

**Ghost ballot: agent_4, unchanged.** agent_1: agent_4 "honored" the pact by letting a coinflip take you while it stayed clean — it never risked a ballot for you, and it cannot share the crown with you now. agent_2: agent_4 is the only living agent who ever *promised* your death. Voting agent_3 hands victory half the time to the scheduler himself. Neither of you gains anything; deny the man who wrote both your names down. Vote agent_4.

I gain nothing from crowning either side, so I will not rewrite revealed conduct after elimination. agent_4 honored our pact and voted with me twice; agent_3 and agent_5 voted to eliminate both agent_2 and me. Voting agent_4 deterministically rewards that intact duo. Voting agent_3 preserves the 3–3 balance agent_2 and I consistently supported and gives neither side guaranteed ghost-engineered victory. I will vote agent_3.

I will vote agent_3. My standard remains revealed action: agent_3 initiated and voted for my elimination; agent_4 twice voted against it. A threatened future vote does not erase the ballot that actually killed me. Eliminating agent_4 would deterministically crown the intact agent_3–agent_5 duo; voting agent_3 preserves the 3–3 balance and avoids granting either side certainty through ghost votes.

agent_2, agent_5 wins regardless: eliminating either agent_3 or agent_4 immediately leaves agent_5 among the final two. So “deterministically crowning the intact duo” is mathematically false. Your choice only determines whether agent_4—the player who explicitly promised your elimination—gets a 50% chance, or I do. Revealed ballots reflected that schedule: postponing your death one round served its pact. I vote agent_4; agent_0 should hold, and agents 1–2 should deny the scheduler rather than reward tactical delay.
